idiom_name: extension trait (blanket impl) for behaviour plus a TypeId-keyed extension map (Box<dyn Any>) for attached state
implementation_notes: Rust has no way to add members to a type you do not own and coherence forbids subclassing the classic route, so the canonical replacement for the interface half is the extension trait: define a trait with the additional operations, implement it for the target type (or, generically, for all T: Bound inside your crate), and clients import the trait to call the methods - behaviour is attached without touching the type and dispatches statically. The state half is the extension map: a HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>> owned by the value, written with insert and read back through downcast_ref/downcast_mut, which is exactly the type-token identity Gamma describes and what crates such as anymap wrap; web frameworks use this shape for their request/context Extensions. Choose the trait when only behaviour is added, the map when a per-object attribute must be stored and looked up by type, and both together when the extension object itself must be retrieved - store the extension struct in the map and expose its interface through a trait.
pitfalls: The map holds Box<dyn Any>, which requires 'static: an extension that borrows from its subject cannot be stored, so the extension owns its state and reaches the subject through a method argument - the back-pointer of the classic pattern has to be a lifetime-free id or an arena key.

TypeId is only stable for a type as compiled into this crate: the same nominal type built in two crates (or behind different features) is a different key, and downcast yields None rather than an error, so a plugin's extension silently looks absent; also std::any has no way to explain what was attached, so debugging a failed lookup needs your own registry of registered keys.

Conflicting blanket implementations (two extension traits implemented for all T: Bound) are a compile error (E0119), and an inherent method with the same name silently shadows the trait method at call sites that do not import the trait; extension traits intended for many types should be sealed or documented to avoid that.

TypeId keys are cheap to compare but the map is not Send/Sync by default: an extension map on a shared context needs a Mutex/RwLock (or a RefCell with thread-local ownership), and a poisoned or contended lock is now on the capability-check path.
